1:
The second of the seven lots drawn at Shiloh falls to Simeon, and every witness treats its oddity — a tribe settled inside another tribe's territory — as the point of the verse. The reformed John Gill fixes the arithmetic first: this is the second of the seven, Benjamin's being the first, since the two lots of Judah and Joseph preceded both.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the arrangement as providence answering an old sentence. For the conduct of Simeon and Levi in the massacre of the Shechemites, Jacob had foretold in the spirit of prophecy that he would divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel; and Clarke finds that most literally fulfilled in how God afterwards disposed of both. Levi was scattered through all Palestine, receiving no inheritance but only cities to dwell in; and Simeon was dispersed in Judah, with what could scarcely be called their own, or a peculiar lot. The reformed John Calvin says the same more sharply — this lot came not as a mark of honour but rather as a mark of disgrace. He notes that Levi's punishment was not merely mitigated but converted into an excellent dignity, his posterity being set on a kind of watch-tower to keep the people in the paths of piety; whereas for Simeon the dispersion Jacob prophesied plainly took place, since although they were not sent off to any great distance, they dwelt scattered, and as strangers in a land properly belonging to another.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry observes the order without softening it. Simeon's lot was drawn after Judah's, Joseph's and Benjamin's because Jacob had put that tribe under disgrace — yet it is put before the two younger sons of Leah and the three sons of the handmaids. And he records what the tribe produced: not one person of note, neither judge nor prophet, that we know of.

Alongside the prophecy the witnesses set a practical cause, and the two do not compete. Henry explains that those who first surveyed the land thought it larger than it was, and supposed it would stretch to give every tribe a share proportionate to what had been carved out for Judah; on closer enquiry it would not reach. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley gives both reasons together — partly to fulfil the threat of scattering, since Simeon had no distinct lot but were as inmates to Judah, and partly because on a more exact survey Judah's portion did far exceed what they needed or what the other tribes could expect. He adds the detail that settles it: this was the least of the tribes, and therefore the fittest to be put within another.

Calvin draws the general lesson from the mistake rather than excusing it. Though the dividers had carefully endeavoured to observe equity, they had fallen into error — and though they were guided by the Spirit, there is nothing strange in their having been partially mistaken, because God sometimes leaves his servants destitute of the spirit of judgment and suffers them to act like men, that they may not plume themselves too much on their clear-sightedness. He adds that the people were punished for their carelessness and confident haste, since they ought at the outset to have ascertained more accurately how much land could properly be assigned to each, and neglected to do it.
2:
Simeon's towns are listed, and the first thing the witnesses notice is that the list will not add up. Gill takes the opening pair as a single name — Beersheba, that is, Sheba — because otherwise there would be fourteen cities where the total given is thirteen; he cites Kimchi and Ben Melech for making them one place, and observes that in the parallel register in Chronicles Sheba is left out and only Beersheba appears. Keil and Delitzsch, reading with grammatical-historical care, reach the same difficulty from the other end: Sheba is wanting in the Chronicles list, and they judge it has no doubt been omitted through a copyist's error, since Shema answers to it in the Judah register, standing before Moladah exactly as Sheba does here. Their summary of the problem is flat — the total of thirteen does not tally, as there are fourteen names.

Most of these places have been met before, and the witnesses say so rather than repeating themselves. Keil and Delitzsch refer the names of the next four verses back to their treatment of the corresponding stretch of Judah's list; Clarke does the same, sending the reader to his notes on the same chapter. What the two of them add here is a handful of individual identifications and the meanings of the names, which between them sketch the country. Beersheba Clarke glosses as the well of the oath. Beth-marcaboth he takes for the house or city of chariots, probably a place where war-chariots and cavalry were kept. Beth-lebaoth is the house or city of lionesses, so called, he supposes, from the number of those animals that bred there — a reading Gill extends, wondering whether there was here a Canaanite temple dedicated to lions, as in Egypt there was a city called Leontopolis whose inhabitants worshipped them and built them temples.

The last two verses of the group take in what lies between the towns. Gill explains that the villages round about are not merely the suburbs adjoining the named cities but the small distinct towns and villages scattered up and down the country. Keil and Delitzsch note that four of the towns — Ain and Rimmon in the south land, Ether and Ashan in the lowlands — had already stood in Judah's register, which is exactly what a tribe settled inside another tribe's territory would produce. The boundary of the whole is Baalath-beer, the Ramah of the south, a place up to which the Simeonite territory extended without itself being assigned to them; it is called simply Baal in Chronicles and is probably the Bealoth of the earlier list, though its site has not been determined. Clarke reads its name as the well of the mistresses, and supposes it so called from some superstitious or impure worship set up there.

Keil and Delitzsch close by ruling out one proposed identification on geographical grounds, and the reasoning shows how these lists are tested. Baalath-beer cannot be the Ramet el Khulil an hour north of Hebron, because the territory of Simeon lay in the Negeb and had only two towns in the lowland, so it cannot possibly have reached into the mountains to a point north of Hebron.
9:
The verse states the arrangement plainly and gives its reason: Simeon's inheritance was taken out of Judah's portion, because Judah's part was too much for them. Gill draws the consequence for the shape of the chapter itself — this is why no description is given of Simeon's border, since that had already been given in the account of Judah's lot. A tribe inside another tribe needs no boundary of its own.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the wording exact: the portion of the children of Judah was too much for them, and therefore the children of Simeon had their inheritance within the inheritance of Judah. What that admits is a correction after the fact. The lot had fallen, the survey had been made, and the result had to be adjusted when it proved that one tribe had been given more land than it could use while another would otherwise have gone without.

Calvin builds his whole comment on how Judah behaved when the adjustment came, and he treats it as the moral centre of the passage. The praise of moderation, he says, is due to the tribe of Judah for not contending that the removal of any part of the inheritance already assigned to them was unjust. They might easily have obtruded the name of God and asserted that it was only by his authority that they had obtained that settlement. But when it was decided by the common consent of all the tribes that more had been given them than they could possess without loss and injury to the others, they immediately desisted from every pretext for disputing the matter.

Calvin then explains why the appeal to divine authority would have been not merely ungenerous but false. Their lot had indeed been determined by God as to its situation; but an error had taken place with regard to its extent, their limits having been fixed by human judgment wider than they ought to have been. To have pleaded God's authority for the surplus would therefore have been to plead it wickedly. Acknowledging instead that it would be wrong to keep what occasioned loss to others, they willingly resign it, give a welcome reception to brethren who must otherwise have remained without any inheritance at all, and submit to share what they had supposed was theirs beyond controversy.

Henry, considering the same transaction, draws the rule out of it: in all such cases errors must be excepted and a review admitted if there be occasion. Though in strictness what fell to Judah's lot was their right against all the world, they would not insist on it once it appeared that another tribe wanted what they had to spare. We must look on the things of others, he says, and not on our own only; the abundance of some must supply the wants of others, that there may be somewhat of an equality — for there may be equity where there is not law.
10:
The third lot brings the register north, and with Zebulun a prophecy comes up for testing. Gill has the border going up westward toward the Mediterranean, and reads it as fulfilling what Jacob and Moses had said, that Zebulun should dwell by the sea and be a haven of ships; he cites Josephus, that the Zebulunites took the land as far as the lake of Gennesaret, about Carmel and the sea. Wesley states the same in its strongest form — this tribe was washed by the midland sea on the west and by the sea of Tiberias on the east, answering Jacob's prophecy that Zebulun should be a haven of ships, trading ships on the great sea and fishing ships on the sea of Galilee. Henry says it in almost the same words.

Calvin makes the fulfilment an argument about revelation itself. An old man, an exile who could not set a foot on his own land, assigned a maritime district to the posterity of his son. What could be more extravagant? Yet now, when the lot assigns them a maritime region, no clearer confirmation of his decision could be desired; it was just as if God were twice thundering from heaven. The tribe therefore does not occupy the shore of its own accord or by human suffrage, but by a divine arrangement fixing its habitation next the sea — so that although men erred in the surveying, the light was always seen shining brightly in the darkness. He presses the distinction Jacob drew between the two brothers as well: Zebulun will travel far and wide, carrying on trade and commerce, while Issachar, remaining in his tents, will cultivate a sedentary life; whence it is probable that Zebulun's coast was provided with harbours and well adapted for commerce, while the children of Issachar were content with their own produce and consumed at home the fruits their labour had raised.

Against all of this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott enters an unembarrassed correction, and it is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Tracing the southern boundary westward from Sarid past Jokneam at the south-east end of the Carmel ridge, he notes that the line does not touch the sea, but leaves room for the territory of Asher to interpose. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result independently: Zebulun's inheritance fell above the plain of Jezreel, between that plain and the mountains of Naphtali, bounded by Asher on the west and north-west, by Naphtali on the north and north-east, by Issachar on the south — and it touched neither the Mediterranean Sea nor the Jordan. They allow the compensation the land itself offered, calling it a very fertile country with the fine broad plain above Nazareth.

On Sarid, the point from which the boundary is traced both ways, nobody is certain. Keil and Delitzsch report Knobel's view that the name, signifying a hole or incision, refers not to a town but to the southern opening of the deep narrow wady coming down from the basin of Nazareth, between two steep mountains; they think the locality suitable enough, but allow that Sarid may instead be one of two heaps of ruins on the south side of the mount of the precipice. Ellicott identifies it flatly with a surviving tell of a similar name.

Henry adds what the tribe would become. Though some places in it were made famous in the Old Testament, especially the mountain on which the trial between God and Baal was held in Elijah's time, it was made much more illustrious in the New: within this lot lay Nazareth, from which our Saviour was called; here was the mountain of the transfiguration, and that coast of the sea of Galilee where Christ preached so many sermons and wrought so many miracles.
12:
The line is now traced back from Sarid in the other direction, and the interest of these verses lies in how much of the country can still be recognised. Gill marks the turn: from Sarid eastward, describing the southern border as it runs from west to east; then along on the east to Gittah-hepher, which he identifies as the birthplace of the prophet Jonah, where Jerome says his grave was shown, a small village in his time two miles from Sepphoris.

Keil and Delitzsch work the same ground with a gazetteer at hand. Chisloth-tabor they explain from Kimchi as meaning the flanks of Tabor, a place on the mountain's side, possibly the same as the Chesulloth that appears in Issachar's list a few verses later, and probably the Xaloth that Josephus places in the great plain — the present village on a rocky height west of Tabor, with many tombs cut in the rock. Daberath they identify with a village at the foot of the same mountain, a place given up to the Levites. Gath-hepher they confirm from Jerome as a small hamlet about two hours north of Nazareth on the road to Tiberias, where the prophet's tomb was shown. Rimmon, another Levitical town, they find preserved in a surviving village two and a half hours north of Nazareth. Eth-kazin and Neah they simply mark unknown.

One phrase in this stretch is not a place-name at all, and Keil and Delitzsch say so: the word attached to Rimmon is not a proper name but a participle with the article standing in for a relative pronoun, meaning bounded off, or pricked off — so the sense is Rimmon, which is marked off to Neah. Ellicott renders the same clause as Remmon that stretcheth to Neah, and corrects the tense of the following verb, which he would read as had gone up to Japhia, a place lying west of the two named before it.

The third verse turns the corner into the north. Gill notes that the border took a circuit from the last place to Hannathon, of which and of the following place he has no account beyond Jerome's bare mention of them as in Zebulun. Keil and Delitzsch judge from the verbs that this verse gives the north-west boundary, since the preceding one had pointed to the east. They identify the valley of Jiphtah-el, at which Zebulun touched Asher, with a large wady rising near a village they take for the Jotapata that Josephus defended so obstinately; and if that is right, then Hannathon is probably Cana of Galilee, the home of Nathanael. Ellicott places Hannathon instead at the north-east corner of the boundary, and reads the valley as the gorge running south-west from it toward the plain. The two accounts of the same corner do not agree, which is the ordinary condition of this register: the line is certain, the points along it are argued.
15:
Zebulun's towns close the third lot, and the closing total is the difficulty. Gill notes that of the first two names we read nowhere else. Keil and Delitzsch take the list one by one and are candid about how little survives. Kattath is probably the Kitron mentioned in Judges alongside Nahalol, but is still unknown; Nahalol may be a village with ruins south-west of Nazareth; Shimron is identified by Knobel with a village whose claim they think improbable; Idalah is placed by one traveller at a spot where a few relics of antiquity are found, though Robinson states the very opposite. Of Bethlehem they are more confident: it has been preserved under its old name in a poor village to the north of the others.

That Bethlehem draws comment from everyone, because of the name it shares. Clarke marks it briefly as a different place from that in which our Lord was born. Wesley says the same. Ellicott goes further and argues a point of identification from it — he thinks it right to refer the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem to this town rather than to the southern one, since the Bethlehem of Judah is called Bethlehem-Judah in Judges and Ruth and Bethlehem-Ephratah in Micah, and is designated Bethlehem simply only where it is impossible to mistake it. He adds the observation that the name is not found in any other tribe.

Then the count. The register says twelve cities, and more than twelve names have been given. Keil and Delitzsch had already flagged the same kind of discrepancy in Simeon's list; here Wesley offers the standing explanation — there are more numbered, but the rest either were not cities properly so called, or were not within this tribe but only bordering on it and belonging to others. Ellicott approaches it from the identifications instead: four of the names have not been traced, and, he suggests, they may not all be names of towns at all. The two answers are not the same. Wesley keeps every name a town and adjusts which tribe owns it; Ellicott allows that the list may contain words that were never town-names.

Gill closes the lot with the formula the chapter uses seven times over — this is the inheritance of the children of Zebulun according to their families — and glosses it simply as what was allotted and then divided according to the number of the families. That is the machinery the whole register describes: a lot to fix which country, and then a division within it proportioned to how many people there were to settle.
17:
The fourth lot falls to Issachar, and Clarke stops on the order rather than the land. It is remarkable, he says, that though Issachar was the elder brother, the lot of Zebulun was drawn first — and that this is the order in which Jacob himself named them, though no reason appears here or there why the younger should be preferred. What strikes him is the agreement of the two: that the apparently fortuitous lot should have distinguished them exactly as the prophetic Jacob did. Known unto God are all his works from the beginning; his influence, Clarke concludes, may be as easily seen in the decision by lot as on the mind of the patriarch who foretold what should befall his children in the latter days.

Ellicott looks at the placing of the two tribes together and finds policy in it. Issachar and Zebulun had been associated with Judah in the same camp and division of the army in the wilderness, an association lasting forty years which must have created many ties between them and their leader. It was no ordinary wisdom, he judges, that placed the descendants of Rachel between Judah on the south and Judah's two associates on the north, to cement the union of all Israel and as far as possible to prevent discord. He carries the observation into the gospels: Mary and Joseph, both of the house of David, are found dwelling in Nazareth, in the tribe of Zebulun, so that north and south alike had part in David and inheritance in David's Son.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why this lot is described differently from the last. In this instance only towns are given, and the boundaries are not delineated except for part of the northern line — though the borders may easily be traced from those of the surrounding tribes. Issachar received for the most part the large and very fertile plain of Jezreel, bounded by Manasseh on the south, by Manasseh and Asher on the west, by Zebulun and further east Naphtali on the north, and by the Jordan on the east. Wesley gives the same reason more briefly: lying between Benjamin on the south and Zebulun on the north, the tribe is described not by its borders, which were the same as theirs, but by some of its cities. Henry sketches the same rectangle, from Jordan in the east to the great sea in the west, and notes that it was a numerous tribe.

The first towns named are among the most famous in the register, and the witnesses linger. Jezreel, Keil and Delitzsch note, was the summer residence of Ahab and his house, standing on a mountain with an extensive and splendid prospect over the great plain that took its name — afterwards called Esdraela, and described in the old gazetteer as lying between Scythopolis and Legio. Clarke fixes it by its neighbours: open country, with Legion to the west, Bethshan to the east, the mountains of Gilboa to the south. Shunem they identify as the home of Abishag, five Roman miles south of Tabor; Clarke remembers it rather as the occasional abode of Elisha and the place where he restored a woman's son to life, and as the camp of the Philistines on the ruinous day when Israel was routed at Gilboa and Saul and his sons were killed. Henry runs through the rest of the tribe's roll of places in the same spirit — the river Kishon where Sisera was beaten, the mountains of Gilboa, the valley of Megiddo where Josiah was slain — so that a bare list of towns becomes a table of contents for the histories that follow.
19:
The middle of Issachar's list is the hardest ground in the chapter for identification, and the witnesses are honest about it. Gill can place the first name from Jerome, who calls it Aphraim, a city of Issachar, and adds that in his own day a village of a similar name stood six miles north of Legion. Of Rabbith he can say only that Jerome calls it Rabboth in this tribe. Of Remeth he offers a cross-reference rather than a site, taking it for the same as the Jarmuth of the Levitical list and the Ramoth of Chronicles.

Keil and Delitzsch work harder and come away with little more. Haphraim they identify with the village Gill's authority points to, on the west of Sulem. Sion, described in the old gazetteer only as a village near Mount Tabor, has not been discovered. Anaharath is placed by Knobel at a village on the eastern side of the Little Hermon — but Knobel regards the text itself as corrupt, and, following one Greek manuscript which gives two names where the Hebrew has one, would emend the reading. Keil and Delitzsch decline: the very circumstance that the manuscript has two names instead of one makes its reading suspicious. Rabbith they report as Knobel's identification with a village at the southern foot of Gilboa. Kishion, given up to the Levites and erroneously written Kedesh in Chronicles, is unknown; so is Abez, which is never mentioned again.

Remeth draws their longest note, and it is an instructive refusal. Knobel, taking the name to signify height, proposed a village on one of the western peaks of Gilboa, since its modern name also means a lofty inaccessible mountain or a castle set on one. Keil and Delitzsch grant that this is certainly not impossible, and then explain why it is improbable: the village evidently got its name because it has the appearance of a fortification when seen from a distance, so the name has nothing in common with the Hebrew word; and the travellers Knobel cites say nothing at all about the ruins he mentions there. Of the whole group only En-gannim is placed with any confidence, and that by its survival — Keil and Delitzsch connect it with the town Josephus calls Ginaea, the present Jenin, and note that the name itself means a fountain of gardens.

Ellicott's contribution to these three verses is almost nothing but a string of modern names and map-sheet numbers, which is its own kind of comment: where he can attach a ruin or a village to a name he does so and says no more. Read together, the three witnesses give a fair picture of what this part of the register is. Most of these places have vanished; some survive under an Arabic form of the old name; a few are argued over on the strength of a supposed etymology, and Keil and Delitzsch are willing to say that such an argument is worth very little.
22:
Issachar's boundary is brought to the Jordan, and the last places on it raise two familiar questions — which Tabor is meant, and whether the total can be trusted. Gill takes Tabor here for the city rather than the mountain, noting that Tabor was the name of a mountain in those parts, generally supposed to be the one on which our Lord was transfigured, though he does not think the evidence sufficient; there was a city of the same name near it, which either gave its name to the mount or received it, and which the Greeks called Itabyrium. He quotes Polybius, who describes it as situated on a hill rising in the form of a breast, with an ascent of more than fifteen furlongs, and calls it a city.

Keil and Delitzsch agree that the mountain is not meant, and then raise a complication. Tabor was a town on the mountain given to the Levites — but given by Zebulun, not by Issachar, according to Chronicles; and it stood on Zebulun's border, as the earlier boundary description shows. Here, however, it appears to be reckoned to Issachar, since otherwise the sixteen cities cannot be made up. They allow that it might have been allotted to Zebulun and still counted here; but they also allow the other possibility, and state it plainly — as there are several discrepancies between the numbers given and the names actually mentioned, it is quite possible that in this instance too the number sixteen is incorrect. On Beth-shemesh, Clarke adds the meaning of the name, the house or temple of the sun, and observes that there were several towns so called in Palestine, which he takes for ample proof that the worship of that luminary had generally prevailed in the country.

Ellicott, having little to identify, notes which of these towns matter later: Shunem and Jezreel are famous in the subsequent history, Shunem especially in the story of Elisha. That is worth setting beside Keil and Delitzsch's caution about the arithmetic, because it marks what the register is and is not. The count of cities may be wrong; the places themselves are where Israel's later history happened.

Gill closes the lot with the same formula the chapter uses at the end of each — this is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Issachar — and glosses it as what fell to them by lot, as before described. Keil and Delitzsch add only that the summary covers the cities and their villages, which is the standing reminder that a tribe's possession was never merely the named towns but the country between them.
24:
The fifth lot runs up the coast, and Keil and Delitzsch describe both the territory and the order of its telling: Asher received the land along the Mediterranean from Carmel to the northern boundary of Canaan itself, and the description begins not at an end but in the middle, in the neighbourhood of Acco, working first southwards and then north. Gill notes only that the lot entitled the tribe to the inheritance next described.

Ellicott looks at the pairing of this tribe with the next and finds a policy in it. Asher and Naphtali had been associated with Dan during the exodus, encamping on the north side of the tabernacle and bringing up the rear of the march; and here the two are paired again in their inheritance, each of them dissociated from his own full brother — Asher from Gad and Naphtali from Dan. He notes the cross-ties that produced: Asher was the more akin to the house of Judah, since Zilpah his mother was Leah's handmaid, and Naphtali to the house of Joseph, since Bilhah was Rachel's. In every case, he judges, the lot fell in such a way as to favour the construction of a united Israel — a body of twelve tribes organised as one.

The first towns are worked over with the usual mixture of confidence and candour. Gill takes Helkath for the same as the Hukok of the Levitical list and reports Masius placing it ten or twelve miles above Ptolemais; Keil and Delitzsch agree about the Levitical town, call the Chronicles form an old copyist's error, and identify it with a Druse village on an eminence three hours east of Acco which the remains show to be an ancient place. Hali may be a village between that place and Acco. Beten, described in the old gazetteer as lying eight Roman miles east of Ptolemais, has not been found. Achshaph is unknown — the gazetteer says only that it was in the tribe of Asher, while a second entry places it at the foot of Tabor, which would put it in Zebulun's country altogether.

Over one identification Keil and Delitzsch lose patience, and the moment is worth recording because it shows how these arguments are weighed. Knobel supposed Amad to be the port south of Acre, identifying it with the sycamore city named by Strabo, Ptolemy and Pliny, on the ground that the Hebrew name resembles the Arabic noun for sycamore — an argument, they remark, the weakness of which does not need to be pointed out. Alammelech they treat more kindly, finding its name preserved in a wady running into the Kishon, since the valley was probably named after a place within it or near it; and Misheal, another Levitical town, they place on the coast near Carmel, which suits the clause that follows.

Carmel itself draws the longest note. Clarke reads the name as the vineyard of God and calls the mountain so fruitful that it passed into a proverb, celebrated above all for the miracles of Elijah; he distinguishes it carefully from the other Carmel in Judah, places it about a hundred and twenty furlongs south of Ptolemais on the edge of the sea, and records that in Vespasian's time a temple stood on it dedicated to a god of the same name. He also weighs the claim of the religious order that took its name from the mountain in Elijah's honour: some pretend it was established by the prophet himself, while others, with more probability, fix its foundation in the twelfth century. Wesley marks the same distinction more briefly — Carmel by the sea, to tell it from Carmel in Judah — and reads its fruitfulness as agreeing with the prophecy concerning Asher.
27:
From the sea the boundary turns inland, and Keil and Delitzsch trace the turn closely. Eastwards from the coast, probably following the river upward for a short distance, it reached Beth-dagon — a place not yet discovered, and one they are careful to distinguish from the similarly named village between Yafa and Ludd. From there it touched Zebulun and the valley of Jiphtah-el on the north of Beth-emek and Neiel, and went out on the left hand of Cabul. What makes the passage useful is that it closes a circuit: the north-west boundary of Asher ran into the valley of Jiphtah-el, the same valley named earlier as the end of Zebulun's line, so that here Asher's eastern boundary touched the north-west corner of Zebulun. The registers of two tribes, written separately, meet at a named ravine.

Clarke explains the odd phrase about the left hand, and it is a small lesson in how the Hebrew describes a country. On the left hand means to the north of Cabul, for so the left hand is understood among the Hebrews when it refers to place — a man giving directions faces the sunrise, so that north lies to his left. Clarke then heads off a confusion with some vigour. This town must not be confounded with the twenty cities Solomon gave Hiram, which the king in his displeasure called the land of Cabul, the paltry land; there was evidently a town of this name long before Solomon's day, and therefore the verse cannot be adduced as an argument that the book of Joshua was written after the time of David. He supposes it the place Josephus mentions as lying by the sea-side near Ptolemais.

The next verse carries the line to the Phoenician frontier, and Keil and Delitzsch note that from here to the end of the lot the towns and boundaries given are those of the northern district, with Sidon, Tyre and Achzib named as the markers. Over the first name in the list they weigh a proposed correction and decline to settle it. Ebron has not been traced; and since Abdon appears among the towns Asher gave up to the Levites, and twenty manuscripts read Abdon here, many writers regard Ebron as a copyist's error. That is possible enough, they allow, but by no means certain — the manuscript reading may easily have arisen from the Levitical list, and since Asher's towns are not all given here in any case, Abdon may simply have been omitted. Gill takes the same view of the two forms, treating Hebron here as the Abdon of the other list, with the change of a letter, and adds that this at least distinguishes it from the far better-known Hebron in Judah.

Sidon closes the group, and the witnesses are struck by what Israel did not get. Clarke observes that the city and the Sidonians are celebrated from the remotest antiquity and frequently mentioned by Homer. Wesley says it is called great for its antiquity, its riches and its glory, and then makes the theological point of the whole northern boundary: the city either was not given to the Israelites or at any rate was never possessed by them — and that, he thinks, not without a singular providence of God, lest by the opportunity of so good a port they should be engaged in much commerce with other nations, and along with the wealth contract their errors and vices.
29:
The northern end of Asher's border runs past two famous cities, and the second of them provokes the sharpest textual argument in the chapter. Gill takes Ramah for a city on the borders of Asher and Naphtali, noting that Jerome distinguishes a Ramah in each tribe, and passes on Masius's conjecture that it is the same as Sarepta. Keil and Delitzsch place it at a village south-east of Tyre where several ancient sarcophagi are still to be seen.

On Tyre, Clarke will not accept the English. He suspects the rendering "the strong city Tyre" is an improper translation, and would keep the Hebrew as it stands — the coast turned to Ramah and to the fortified city, mibtsar tsor. Our translators here left the Hebrew and followed the Greek and Latin versions, he says, a fault of which they are sometimes guilty. His objection is historical. The famous city of Tyre was not known until about two hundred years after Joshua's day; and Homer, who mentions Sidon and the Sidonians frequently, never mentions Tyre at all — a proof, in Clarke's judgement, that the city afterwards so eminent was not then known. The word itself signifies a rock or strong place, and since there were many rocks in Judea which with a little art were made into strongholds, several places might carry the name.

Keil and Delitzsch reach a similar destination by a different road, without disputing the translation: the fortified town meant here is not insular Tyre but the town on the mainland, the present Sur, standing by the coast in a beautiful and fertile plain. Wesley agrees, and adds that the boundary reached Tyre exclusively, since the city formed no part of the land given to Israel; and both he and Henry pass on the same conjecture, which Henry credits to Bishop Patrick — that this old strong city on the continent was not the Tyre of later fame, which was built on an island, and that into these two strongholds many of the people of Canaan fled and took shelter when Joshua invaded them. Clarke supplies the detail that makes the distinction vivid: the celebrated Tyre was a rock in the sea some six or seven hundred paces from the mainland, and to reduce it Alexander was obliged to fill up the channel between.

The lot closes with a total that will not balance and a country that plainly did. Clarke counts nearly thirty cities in the enumeration where the text says twenty-two, and explains the surplus as frontier towns which the border merely passed by, belonging to other tribes and therefore named without being counted; perhaps, he adds, some villages are named as well as cities. Wesley gives the same explanation in a sentence. Against the untidy arithmetic Gill sets the quality of the ground: a goodly heritage, and, according to the prediction of Jacob and Moses, a very fruitful country. He quotes Josephus, that the country from Carmel called the valley — because it was one — fell to the Asherites all the way over against Sidon, with Lebanon on the north, Naphtali on the east, Zebulun to the south and south-east, and the sea to the west.
32:
The sixth lot reaches the top of the country. Henry sets it out first: Naphtali lay furthest north of all the tribes, bordering on Lebanon, with Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west; and the city of Leshem lay on the utmost northern edge of it, so that when the Danites afterwards made themselves masters of that place and called it Dan, the length of Canaan came to be reckoned from Dan to Beersheba. He notes what happened in this tribe and what would happen: near the waters of Merom Joshua had fought and routed Jabin, and within its bounds stood Capernaum and Bethsaida at the north end of the sea of Tiberias, where Christ did so many mighty works.

Calvin reads the allotment against Jacob's blessing, as he has done with Zebulun, and finds the tribe's character in the words Naphtali is a hind let loose; he giveth goodly words. It is worth noting that his own text carries a correction of the geography he builds on it: Calvin supposed the tribe contiguous on one side to the children of Judah and surrounded on the others by the enclosures of their brethren, whereas Judah and Naphtali lie at opposite extremities of the land with five tribes between them, and Naphtali, stretching from the lake of Gennesaret north to the roots of Lebanon, formed the extreme frontier rather than an inland enclosure. He also observes that in the statement that the tribe of Dan took Leshem there seems to be a tacit comparison drawn between the two.

The boundary description is unusually hard to follow, and Keil and Delitzsch say so before they begin: the lines are given, but with the uncertainty that attaches to several of the places named, they cannot be traced with certainty. Gill marks the northern coast as running from west to east and ending at the Jordan, and admits of its first point that though it lay to the north, it cannot be said expressly what it was or where. Keil and Delitzsch render the line as running from Heleph, from the oak-forest at Zaanannim, by Adami of the pass and Jabneel to Lakkum, with its outgoings at the Jordan; they place the oak-forest near Kedesh north-west of Lake Huleh, and note that there are still many oaks in that neighbourhood. Ellicott takes almost the opposite view of where these places lie — all of them except Heleph, on his identifications, lie near the Sea of Galilee on its south-west side — and fixes the eastern border as the Jordan, taking in the waters of Merom and the Sea of Galilee.

The southern line produces a genuine textual problem, and nobody solves it. Wesley explains the direction of travel — the northern border was drawn from west to east, which is why the next verse turns from the east westward. But that verse ends by touching "Judah upon Jordan," and Clarke states the difficulty flatly: it is certain that Naphtali did not border on Judah, for several tribes lay between them. Some think that since both tribes were bounded by Jordan on the east they might be considered in some sort conjoined; but that, he objects, might be said of several other tribes too. If with the Greek version we omit Judah the difficulty vanishes, though no manuscript supports the omission; and Houbigant, who calls the words meaningless as they stand, proposed reading instead by the banks of Jordan. Ellicott, offered all of this, says only that of Judah upon Jordan we can say nothing with certainty.
35:
Naphtali's towns are introduced by a phrase used of no other tribe here, and Ellicott catches it: these are the fenced cities — observe, he says, the protection of the northern border by fortresses. A frontier tribe is given a frontier's furniture.

The identifications run from the confident to the frankly hopeless. Gill reports from the Talmud that Ziddim was later called the village of wheat, perhaps from the quantity or the quality of the wheat grown there. Keil and Delitzsch call it unknown, and reject Knobel's proposed site on a geographical ground they use repeatedly — the ruin he suggests lies west of the Wady Bessum, which puts it in the territory of Issachar rather than Naphtali. Zer they also give up; the Greek and Syriac read the name as Zor, and Knobel connects it with a ruin at the south end of the lake which he takes for the Taricheae of Josephus, a proposal Keil and Delitzsch dismiss in three words as a very doubtful combination. Hammath, whose name means hot springs, they place near the later city of Tiberias on the western shore, no doubt the village with warm baths that Josephus mentions. Wesley adds the one name every reader will know already: Chinnereth, from which the lake of Gennesaret took its name.

Further north the ground is better. Keil and Delitzsch describe Ramah as the present Rameh, a large well-built village inhabited by Christians and Druses, surrounded by extensive olive plantations and provided with an excellent well, standing on a mountain slope in a beautiful plain — and then add, with characteristic honesty, that it has no relics of antiquity at all. Gill identifies Kedesh as the Kedesh in Galilee in Mount Naphtali, distinguished by that title from others of the name, and one of the cities of refuge; Jerome knew it as Cidissus, twenty miles from Tyre. Adamah, Edrei and En-hazor are variously guessed at; of En-hazor Keil and Delitzsch note that the ruins on the likeliest site are merely those of an ordinary village with one broken cistern. Over Hazor itself Ellicott reports that previous writers have identified it variously, but that Conder expresses no doubt, since his site occupies a commanding position above a stream flowing into Lake Merom.

One proposal is examined and refused at length, and the refusal is instructive. Migdal-el might, so far as the name goes, be the Magdala on the western shore of the lake — except that the towns on that lake have already been listed. Knobel therefore joined Migdal-el to the following name, making one town of two, and found it in a village west of Rameh. Keil and Delitzsch answer that there is nothing whatever to favour the combination except a similarity of sound, and two things against it: the village lies so far west, barely three hours from Acre, that Naphtali can hardly have reached it. Then comes the total, and with it the usual discrepancy — Clarke counts twenty-three cities where the text says nineteen, and explains the excess as before, by frontier towns belonging to other tribes. Gill closes the lot with Josephus, who gives the tribe the country eastward as far as Damascus and upper Galilee, up to Lebanon and the fountains of Jordan that flow out of the mountain.
40:
The seventh and last lot falls to Dan, and every witness reads the delay and the position together. Gill notes simply that this was the last lot drawn. Henry finds the arrangement pointed: Dan commanded one of the four squadrons of the camp in the wilderness — the one that brought up the rear — and yet was last provided for in Canaan; and his portion fell in the south, between Judah on the east and the land of the Philistines on the west, Ephraim to the north and Simeon to the south. Providence, he judges, ordered this numerous and powerful tribe into a post of danger, as the tribe best able to deal with those vexatious neighbours — and so it was found in Samson.

Ellicott presses the same reading with the census figures behind it. Dan was the most numerous tribe next to Judah at every count taken during the exodus, and had held a post of honour in commanding the rear-guard on the march; a similar post is assigned here, next to Judah on the side of the Philistine territory. Since the Philistines were the most powerful and warlike of the unconquered nations, the wisdom of guarding Israel's frontier with the two strongest tribes is manifest. He follows the arrangement forward to its result: it was Samson, a Danite, who began to deliver Israel from them, and David who completed the work.

Keil and Delitzsch explain how the territory was assembled, and it is unlike the others. Dan's inheritance fell west of Benjamin, between Judah and Ephraim, and was formed by Judah giving up some of its northern towns and Ephraim some of its southern ones, so as to furnish a territory proportionate to the tribe's number. It lay mostly in the lowland, taking in the hill country between the sea and the mountains and part of the plain of Sharon, so that it belonged to one of the most fruitful portions of the land. As with Issachar, the boundaries are not given, because they could be traced from those of the adjoining tribes. Wesley and Gill both make the same observation from the other side — this tribe is described by its cities and not its borders, which were in part the same as Judah's, and its inheritance was in good part taken out of Judah's too large portion, as several of the towns named here show, since they were reckoned in Judah's list as well.

Ellicott raises a question about those shared names that the register does not answer. Zorah and Eshtaol, and Ekron too, had been originally assigned to Judah; and it is not clear whether they are mentioned here as marking the border between Dan and Judah or as actually lying in Danite territory. Keil and Delitzsch supply a complication of their own: of Zorah, Eshtaol and Ir-shemesh the Danites did not in fact take possession, since Judah had given them up to the Levites. Two more of the towns, they note, remained in the hands of the Canaanites altogether, and both turn up later in the histories — one repeatedly in the wars of David and Solomon, the other fortified by Rehoboam and afterwards taken by the Philistines. Clarke, glossing Ir-shemesh as the city of the sun, calls the name another proof of the idolatry of the Canaanites. Dan, as Ellicott sums it up, is wedged in between two powerful tribes, the unconquered Philistines and the sea.
43:
The rest of Dan's towns run down toward the coast, and the list is a mixture of famous names and blanks. Gill's refrain through this stretch is that of such and such a place we read nowhere else — of Elon, of Jehud, of the two whose names open the last verse of the group. Where he can attach a place he does: Shaalabbin he takes for the Shaalbim of Judges, which Jerome knew as a large village on the borders of Sebaste under a similar name; Eltekeh he identifies as a city given to the Levites, and reports the supposition that it is the same as a town of a like name in Judah handed over to the Danites.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the same names through the later histories, which is where these obscure places acquire their interest. Eltekeh and Gibbethon, both Levitical towns, have not been discovered; but Gibbethon was in Philistine hands under the earliest kings of Israel, and two royal assassinations happened at its siege. Baalath was fortified by Solomon, and Josephus places it in the neighbourhood of Geser; they take it for the same as the Baalah on Judah's border. Jehud they find preserved in a village two hours north of Ludd, in a splendidly cultivated plain; Bene-berak in another an hour from it; Gath-rimmon, another Levitical town, is described in the old gazetteer as a very large village twelve Roman miles from Diospolis on the road to Eleutheropolis, though it has not been found. Clarke adds the meanings where he can — Shaalabbin, the foxes, a city of which the Amorites kept constant possession; Ekron, a well-known city of the Philistines and the metropolis of one of their five dynasties — and notes that Ajalon had a namesake about two miles from Nicopolis on the road to Jerusalem.

The last verse of the group ends the list at the sea, and produces the most interesting problem in it. Me-jarkon and Rakkon, whose first name Keil and Delitzsch render as the waters of yellowness, are unknown; but the clause that follows — with the territory before Japho — fixes them near Joppa, since that phrase takes in the places in the environs of the port. From which they draw an inference that sits awkwardly with the later history: Joppa itself does not appear to have belonged to the territory of Dan, although according to the song of Deborah the Danites must have had possession of the town. So the register stops just short of the harbour, and the poem assumes they held it.

Clarke, characteristically, closes on what the port became rather than what the boundary did. Japho is the place since called Joppa, lying on the Mediterranean, and the chief seaport in the possession of the twelve tribes — which is a large claim to rest on a boundary that, by Keil and Delitzsch's reading, may not quite have reached it.
47:
The register breaks off into a piece of narrative, and the witnesses divide over the very first clause. The English says the coast of the children of Dan went out too little for them. Clarke concedes that this is the meaning, but points out that the translators had to add the words to produce it, and reports Houbigant's conjecture that a copyist, familiar with the recurring formula of the boundary lists, wrote it here in place of a phrase meaning that the border was strait for them. Ellicott takes the harder line: the words are not in the original, and it is better to translate literally — the coast of the children of Dan went out from them, that is, their territory was partly re-conquered. Gill offers both readings and inclines the same way, noting that leaving out the supplement gives "it went out from them," so that they lost part of what they had, being driven out of the valley into the mountain by the Amorites, which obliged them to look elsewhere for room.

Ellicott builds the whole passage on that reading, and his verdict on the Danites is the severest in the chapter. Something similar, he says, seems to have happened in several districts: the Israelites did not take advantage of the impression Joshua's victories had produced, so the nations of Canaan repossessed their former abodes and held them. Dan and Judah, numerically the two strongest tribes at every census, had been placed next to the Philistines with the task of conquering them, and it was not effected; the Amorites forced the children of Dan into the mountains. Hence, he concludes, instead of attacking the Philistines and Amorites in the inheritance actually given them, the Danites preferred to form a new settlement far in the north, and put to the sword a people quiet and secure who had no deliverer, rather than run with patience the race set before them.

Wesley reads the same migration more sympathetically and answers a different question — why the notice stands here at all. It was done after Joshua's death, and seems inserted so that all the chief places where the Danites dwelt, though far distant from each other, might be mentioned together; and to account for so strange an accident as their removing from an appointed portion to so remote a place. Being much molested by bad neighbours they thought fit to go somewhere remote from them, and were in a manner constrained to it, since otherwise they must have taken part of another tribe's portion, whereas by going to the utmost northern point of the land they took what belonged to no other tribe at all. Keil and Delitzsch give the same sequence without the judgement: after Joshua's death the Danites of Zorah and Eshtaol conquered Leshem and gave it the name of Dan, because the territory allotted them was too small, owing to their inability to drive the Amorites out of several of their towns.

That the paragraph describes something later than the book's own narrative is admitted on all sides, and Clarke states the consequence plainly: it must be granted that the whole account in this verse refers to a fact which did not take place till after the death of Joshua, and it is another of those marginal or explicative notes added by a later hand. He fixes the place as well — near the origin of Jordan, at the utmost northern extremity of the land as Beersheba was at the southern, which is the origin of the standing expression from Dan even to Beersheba — and rejects the supposition that Leshem was Caesarea Philippi. Keil and Delitzsch identify it with the mound at the central source of the Jordan. Gill closes the lot by boxing the tribe in on all four sides: Ephraim north, Judah east, Simeon south, the Mediterranean west.
49:
The division is finished, and the last inheritance given is the leader's own. Gill names the commissioners — Eleazar, Joshua and the ten men appointed — and dates the grant to the moment when all the lots had been drawn and each tribe's portion divided among its families.

Henry and Calvin both fasten on the order, and neither thinks it accidental. Joshua was served last, though the greatest man in Israel, and one who, having commanded in the conquest, might have demanded the first settlement for himself; but he would make it appear that in everything he sought the good of his country and not his own interest. He was content to be unfixed until he saw them all settled — an example, Henry says, to everyone in public place, to prefer the common welfare to their own satisfaction. Calvin puts it as a question: how seldom do we find any who, after giving one or two specimens of valour, do not forthwith make haste to the prey? In the delay, he says, there was a striking proof of this holy servant's moderation, since he gives no heed to his own interest until the commonwealth has been secured.

The same temperance is conspicuous in what he asked for. Calvin describes the city Joshua requested as a mere heap of stones, either because it had been demolished or because no city had yet been built on the site, and thinks it probable that he chose something of no great value in order to make the grant as little invidious as possible. Clarke agrees from another direction, reporting that Timnath-serah — called Timnath-heres in Judges, where the mountain it stood on is named — is generally allowed to have been a barren spot in a barren country. Wesley explains what building it means: not founding but repairing and enlarging, in the sense in which Nebuchadnezzar is said to have built Babylon. Calvin adds, against the objection that Joshua should have served for nothing, that the grant was no wage but a testimonial of the divine power exercised through his hand.

Two smaller points are contested. The first is who gave it. The text says the children of Israel gave Joshua his inheritance, which Henry takes for a mark of humility, since he would not take it without the people's consent; Wesley explains the phrase constitutionally — the land had been given to Joshua, Eleazar and the princes as joint trustees acting for the people, so that even Joshua could take nothing except by their gift. The second is what "according to the word of the LORD" refers to. Gill allows two possibilities, either the oracle of Urim and Thummim consulted by Eleazar, or what the Lord had said to Moses when Hebron was ordered to Caleb. Keil and Delitzsch reject the first outright: the phrase does not refer to a divine oracle communicated through the high priest, but to a promise Joshua had probably received at the same time as Caleb, at Kadesh, and which, like Caleb's, is not recorded in the books of Moses. Henry takes the same view, and finds it what made the portion doubly pleasant — that Joshua had it not as the rest did by common providence, but by special promise. He adds one observation about the site: Joshua chose it in Mount Ephraim, within his own tribe, putting himself in common with them when he might have distinguished himself by settling elsewhere; and the tabernacle stood in Ephraim's lot, so that he would forecast not to be far from it.

Clarke closes the division on the method rather than the men. All the inheritances were determined by lot, and the lot was cast before the LORD at the door of the tent, as under his eye. Hence, he observes, there was no murmuring, each tribe having received its inheritance as from the hand of God himself.
